headline: Mission Complete — Finding Weaknesses, Not Victims
message:
Monday, 3:41 PM. The engagement log had a new section.

--- VULNERABILITY ASSESSMENT COMPLETE ---

45.77.180.10 — Development Server:
22/tcp   OpenSSH 7.4 — CVE research complete. No critical findings in this version range. Low-severity CVEs noted.
80/tcp   Apache httpd 2.4.49 — CVE-2021-41773 (CVSS 9.8). C: Confirmed — version in affected range. P: Inconclusive — mod_cgi status not determinable from external position. R: Confirmed — port accessible, no WAF filtering detected. STATUS: Potential critical finding. Internal configuration verification required.
443/tcp  Apache httpd 2.4.49 — Same as 80/tcp above. Four Apache 2.4.49 instances share this finding.
3306/tcp [filtered — version unknown] — CVE research not possible. Version undetermined. Status: active unknown.

45.77.180.11 — Legacy Server:
22/tcp   OpenSSH 7.4 — Same as development server. No critical findings.
80/tcp   Apache httpd 2.4.49 — CVE-2021-41773 as above.
8443/tcp Apache Tomcat 7.0.37 — CVE research complete. Multiple CVEs in 7.0.x range. End-of-life status: no further patches will be issued. High-severity CVEs identified requiring further validation.

Maya read through the entries. James had his pen ready.

'So CVE-2021-41773 is our most urgent finding,' he said. 'Because of the CVSS score.'

'It is our most urgent investigation,' Maya said. 'Whether it is confirmed depends on mod_cgi.' She looked at the entry for port 8443. 'The Tomcat situation is also serious — not because of one headline CVE, but because end-of-life software accumulates risk. No patches coming, ever. Every future CVE in that product line applies to this server with no remediation path except upgrade.'

James looked at the Apache entries across both servers. 'And if CVE-2021-41773 is confirmed — mod_cgi is enabled — then it is on both servers. Four ports.'

'Which is why,' Maya said, 'the next question is not which one to exploit. The next question is: how do we verify safely?' She closed the NVD tab and turned to face him. 'Exploitation is not a casual action. Done incorrectly, it crashes services, corrupts data, triggers alerts, or causes real harm to a system you do not own. Professional validation requires technique, planning, and boundaries — exactly as clear as the authorisation letter that gave us permission to be here in the first place.'

James was quiet for a moment. 'So we know what the weaknesses are.'

'We know what they probably are,' Maya said. 'That is the honest answer. We know which CVEs are potential matches. We know which prerequisites need to be confirmed. We have an evidence-based, prioritised finding list with the limitations clearly documented.' She leaned back. 'That is what professional vulnerability assessment produces. Not certainty — structured uncertainty. Documented, defensible, actionable.'

She looked at the engagement log and then at him.

'We have identified the weaknesses. Now comes the most important question a penetration tester can ask.'

She paused.

'How do professionals verify a vulnerability safely — without damaging the target?'

---

In this mission, you crossed from 'we have version numbers' to 'we have a prioritised, evidence-based vulnerability picture.'

You learned that a version match in the CVE database is a hypothesis — not a finding. A finding requires CPR: confirming the version range, checking the prerequisites, and verifying reachability. A vulnerability that fails any one of these three checks is not a confirmed finding, regardless of its CVSS score.

You learned that CVSS is a starting indicator — the worst-case severity in a reference scenario. It tells you what to investigate first. It does not tell you what you will find. A 9.8 with prerequisites absent may be a 7.5 or a false positive. A 5.8 on an unprotected, internet-facing, revenue-critical asset may deserve higher urgency than a 9.8 on an isolated test server.

You learned what CVE, CWE, CVSS, CPE, and NVD each mean — why they were created, what they measure, and how professionals use them together. Vulnerability research is not searching for alarming numbers. It is building an evidence trail from version string to documented risk.

The Meridian Financial engagement now has a prioritised finding list: CVE-2021-41773 on four Apache instances awaiting mod_cgi verification, Tomcat 7.0.37 on an end-of-life version with multiple CVEs, and an unknown service on a filtered database port requiring follow-up.

Mission 5 begins at the next professional question: how do we confirm these findings through controlled, safe validation — without becoming the incident we were hired to prevent?

badgesUnlocked.name: Vulnerability Analyst
badgesUnlocked.description: Completed Mission 4: Finding Weaknesses, Not Victims — conducted a professional vulnerability assessment of the Meridian Financial service map. Researched CVEs for all confirmed service versions using the NVD, interpreted CVSS scores in context rather than as action orders, applied the CPR framework to distinguish potential matches from confirmed findings, and produced an evidence-based, prioritised vulnerability picture for Mission 5.

nextSteps: Mission 5: Professional Validation & Controlled Exploitation — CVE-2021-41773 is flagged for the Apache instances on both servers. The mod_cgi prerequisite must be confirmed or ruled out. Mission 5 introduces the professional methodology for validating vulnerability findings through controlled, safe, evidence-based techniques — without causing unintended damage to the target environment.

Optional: Return to the vulnerability research lab and practise applying CPR to at least five different CVEs across different software types. For each one, find a scenario where the finding would be a false positive — and document exactly which CPR question revealed it.

Review: The CPR framework — Confirm, Prerequisites, Reachability — is the professional standard of care for every CVE match in every engagement. Apply it before any finding enters a report. The CVSS score determines where to start. Evidence determines what the report says.
